strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored setting: human-AI collaboration with continuous control, object physics, collision constraints, and behaviors such as joint carrying, handoff, and deciding when help is needed. The proposed Moving Out benchmark is a useful step beyond grid-world or task-level collaboration environments.

The benchmark design is reasonably concrete, with 12 maps organized around coordination, awareness, and action-consistency modes, and the manuscript provides useful metric definitions for task completion, normalized progress, waiting time, and force alignment.

The paper includes human-human data collection and a human-AI user study, which are valuable for this topic. The IRB approval and compensation are reported, and the limitations section honestly notes that the environment does not cover all physical interactions and that generative policy inference speed remains challenging.

BASS is a practical and intuitive combination of behavior augmentation, next-state prediction, and action selection. Across reported AI-AI experiments, it improves over MLP/GRU/diffusion/MAPPO baselines on TCR and NFD, and the ablations suggest both augmentation and simulation can help, especially when added to diffusion policies.
The paper is generally understandable and includes implementation details, reward settings, metric formulas, compute information, and additional map descriptions in the appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough to fully support the broad claims. The environment is a 2D game-like simulator, yet the paper repeatedly frames conclusions around physically grounded human-AI collaboration and embodied agents more generally. The evaluation does not establish transfer beyond Moving Out, apart from a brief one-sentence Overcooked result with little detail.

There are serious consistency and reproducibility issues. The main text says the human subject study used 32 participants, while Appendix I says 12 volunteers. The abstract says a project page is available but no URL appears in the extracted manuscript. Code, data splits, random seeds, exact train/test partitioning, and the action-candidate generation procedure for BASS are not specified sufficiently for reliable reproduction.

The behavior recombination augmentation may create physically inconsistent trajectories: partner sub-trajectories are swapped while environment/object states are retained from the original trajectory, and the paper explicitly says validation is not required. This weakens the soundness of the claim that the generated trajectories are valid demonstrations of collaborative behavior.

The BASS method is somewhat incremental: data augmentation plus learned dynamics model plus one-step action scoring is plausible but not highly novel. The paper would need more careful analysis to show why this particular formulation is necessary, when it fails, and how it compares to stronger model-predictive or imitation-learning alternatives.

The human-AI evaluation is underreported. It mainly compares DP to BASS, with unclear sample size, unclear counterbalancing/statistical analysis, and only one reported p-value for vaguely described questionnaire differences. Objective human-AI metrics are shown in a figure but not tabulated with uncertainty or statistical tests.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. MAPPO is trained with dense shaped rewards and special map-specific reward modifications, while BC methods use human data; the comparison mixes different training signals and does not clearly separate benchmark difficulty from implementation choices. Human-play comparisons against RL baselines are absent.

Reported performance remains modest: even the best BASS variants achieve TCR around 0.50 on Task 1 and 0.43 on Task 2 in the appendix tables. This supports the benchmark's difficulty, but it makes the claimed effectiveness of BASS feel overstated.

Presentation has several polish problems, including typos such as BAAS/Diffuson, grammatical issues, missing project-page URL, and table/appendix inconsistencies. These are not fatal individually, but they compound the reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The paper targets an important gap: human-AI collaboration under continuous control, physical constraints, and diverse partner behavior, which is less studied than grid/discrete environments such as Overcooked-AI.

The proposed Moving Out environment is a potentially useful benchmark direction, with multiple map types intended to exercise coordination, awareness of assistance needs, and sustained joint action consistency.
The authors collected human-human demonstrations and included a human-AI study, which is valuable for this topic and preferable to relying only on self-play evaluation.

BASS is simple and modular: behavior augmentation plus learned next-state prediction/action selection can be added to several behavior-cloning backbones, and the paper includes some ablations across GRU and diffusion-policy variants.
weaknesses: The central claims are not convincingly supported. The environment is described as physically grounded and realistic, but it is a simplified 2D physics game; the paper does not establish that success in this setting transfers to embodied robotics or to broader physical collaboration.

The method is technically shallow relative to the claims. BASS selects actions using a myopic predicted next state scored by distance-to-goal/NFD, which is also one of the evaluation metrics. This makes the improvement partly metric-aligned rather than clear evidence of better physical understanding or human adaptation.

The dynamics model evidence is weak. Reported prediction/action-selection accuracy is only about 0.625 on Task 1 and 0.487 on Task 2, and the oracle simulator gap is substantial in Task 2. There is no careful analysis of compounding error, uncertainty, or failure modes of using a learned predictor for action selection.

The behavior augmentation procedure may generate invalid or physically inconsistent trajectories, and the manuscript explicitly says it can improve performance even without explicit validation. This leaves a major soundness gap for a method whose motivation is physical consistency.

The experimental design has serious inconsistencies. The main text says the human subject study used 32 participants, while Appendix I says 12 volunteers. This discrepancy directly affects confidence in the user-study results.

The human study analysis is under-specified and statistically weak: it compares mainly BASS to DP, gives only a single p-value for survey differences, lacks clear correction for multiple questionnaire items, and provides limited details about randomization, counterbalancing, participant overlap with data collection, and train/test separation.

The main quantitative results are modest and not always aligned with the narrative. Full BASS is not consistently best across all backbones/metrics, waiting time sometimes worsens despite being a key metric, and many improvements appear within or near reported standard errors without adequate significance testing.

Baselines are not fully convincing. MAPPO uses dense, hand-shaped rewards and even map-specific reward modifications, making comparison to dataset-driven methods difficult; stronger human-AI coordination baselines and modern offline/interactive imitation or planning methods are missing.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark paper. The abstract's project-page sentence is incomplete, and the manuscript does not clearly commit to releasing code, data, environment, splits, or human-study materials. Hyperparameters are partially reported, but important implementation details for data splits, action candidate generation, and evaluation protocol remain unclear.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for ICML. There are grammatical errors, typos, incomplete text, notation issues in the Dec-MDP formulation, and inconsistent terminology/numbers. These issues are not merely cosmetic because they obscure experimental setup and evidence.

The limitations section is honest but too narrow. It discusses inference speed and environment coverage, but does not adequately address benchmark validity, simplified physics, potential dataset bias, human-study limitations, or ethical/privacy details for collected human behavior data.

strengths: The paper introduces a useful and timely benchmark for physically grounded human-AI collaboration, with continuous control, 2D physics, heterogeneous movable objects, narrow passages, and several collaboration modes such as handoff, assistance, collision avoidance, and joint rotation. This fills a real gap between discrete coordination benchmarks such as Overcooked-AI and more task-level embodied simulators.

The manuscript includes a nontrivial human-human dataset: over 1,000 demonstrations from 36 participants for behavior diversity and 720 expert demonstrations with randomized object properties for physical generalization. The two proposed tasks are well motivated and make the benchmark more than just an environment release.

BASS is a sensible and practically motivated method. The behavior augmentation and dynamics-based action selection components directly target the stated challenges of diverse human partners and constrained physical transitions.

The empirical results are broadly convincing in direction: BASS improves over MLP, GRU, diffusion policy, and MAPPO on task completion and normalized distance, and the paper includes ablations showing that augmentation and simulation both contribute. The human-AI study and subjective feedback add important evidence beyond AI-AI self-play.

The paper is generally well organized, with useful appendices covering metrics, baseline details, MAPPO rewards, compute, data collection, and map descriptions. The limitations section acknowledges remaining failures and incomplete coverage of possible physical interactions.
weaknesses: The benchmark contribution is stronger than the algorithmic novelty. BASS combines fairly standard data augmentation, learned dynamics prediction, and one-step action selection using a distance-to-goal score. The paper should more clearly distinguish what is technically new from what is an effective engineering combination for this benchmark.

There are notable inconsistencies in the human study description. The main text says 32 participants evaluated BASS against DP and each played 32 maps, while Appendix I says 12 volunteers selected among four model IDs and played all twelve maps per model. This weakens confidence in the human-study protocol and statistical analysis.

The statistical treatment is limited. The paper reports one p-value for survey differences but does not clearly specify which comparisons it applies to, whether tests were paired or independent despite a likely within-subject design, or whether multiple-comparison correction was used across survey questions and metrics.

The generated trajectory augmentation is under-validated. The authors state that recombined trajectories can be checked for invalid states or collisions, but also say they improve performance even without explicit validation. For a physically grounded benchmark, this raises concerns that some training data may be physically inconsistent.

The human-AI evaluation is relatively narrow: it mainly compares BASS to diffusion policy rather than the full set of baselines, and the reported subjective results do not provide enough detail on variance, effect sizes, or per-task breakdowns. This limits how strongly one can conclude that BASS generally improves collaboration with real humans.

Reproducibility is adequate but not fully satisfying. Many hyperparameters and data collection details are provided, but the abstract has an empty project-page placeholder, release status for code/data is unclear, and some implementation choices, such as candidate action generation and partner action prediction variants, need more precise specification.

Performance remains modest in absolute terms: even full BASS reaches only about 0.50 TCR on Task 1 and 0.43 TCR on Task 2 in the appendix tables. This is acceptable for a challenging benchmark, but the claims about effective collaboration should be tempered accordingly.

strengths: Introduces a timely benchmark for physically grounded human-AI collaboration with continuous control, physics constraints, diverse object properties, and multiple collaboration modes. This fills a real gap between symbolic settings such as Overcooked-AI and more expensive embodied simulators.

The dataset is a meaningful contribution: over 1,000 human-human demonstrations from 36 participants for behavior diversity and 720 expert demonstrations with randomized physical attributes for physical generalization. The paper also reports IRB approval and participant compensation.

BASS is a sensible and effective combination of behavior augmentation, learned dynamics prediction, partner action prediction, and action reranking. The empirical gains over MLP, GRU, MAPPO, and Diffusion Policy are consistent across TCR, NFD, waiting time, and action consistency.

The paper includes useful ablations and diagnostics: component ablations, oracle simulator comparison, sampling strategy analysis, partner-action ablation, dynamics-model comparisons, and failure-case analysis. These improve confidence that both augmentation and simulation-based action selection contribute.

The presentation is generally clear, with intuitive task descriptions, metrics tailored to physical collaboration, and a helpful appendix that explains data collection, implementation, and map design.
weaknesses: The main evaluation protocol for Task 1 is only a proxy for human-AI generalization: agents trained on disjoint human groups are evaluated against each other. This is reproducible, but it does not fully test adaptation to real unseen humans, and the paper sometimes treats this proxy as stronger evidence than it is.

The human-study reporting is inconsistent: the main text says 32 participants played 32 maps, while Appendix R states 12 volunteers and describes selecting model IDs A-D. This discrepancy materially affects confidence in the human-AI claims and statistical conclusions.

The method originality is moderate. BASS largely combines known ingredients: diffusion-policy sampling, data augmentation, learned dynamics/world models, and model-predictive action selection. The benchmark/dataset is more novel than the algorithmic contribution.

Baselines are somewhat limited for the human-AI collaboration claim. MAPPO is not a strong human-adaptive baseline in this setup, and the paper does not compare against stronger zero-shot coordination or human-modeling methods adapted to the continuous setting, beyond standard BC/RL baselines.

Some methodological details remain underspecified or weakly justified. The trajectory recombination validity relies on discretized start/end matching and a claimed 99% validity rate, but the validation procedure is not described enough to rule out subtle physically implausible or causally inconsistent augmented trajectories.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The abstract has an unfinished project-page sentence, and it is unclear whether the environment, datasets, trained models, and human-study interface will be released. Hyperparameters are provided, but full reproducibility depends heavily on these artifacts.

The empirical performance, while improved, remains modest in absolute terms on AI-AI evaluation, with task completion rates often around 0.3-0.5. This suggests the benchmark is challenging, but also limits how far the practical collaboration claims can be taken.

The significance of Task 2 generalization is somewhat constrained: physical variations are relatively small for pose/mass/size in places, and the environment is still 2D with simplified physics. The paper should be more careful about extrapolating to embodied robots or real-world collaboration.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: human-AI collaboration under physical constraints and continuous control, where existing benchmarks such as Overcooked-style grid worlds are limited.

The proposed Moving Out benchmark has several attractive ingredients: multiple collaboration modes, continuous low-level actions, physics-based object interaction, randomized object properties, and collected human-human demonstrations.
The manuscript includes a reasonably broad set of baselines and metrics, plus ablations for BASS components, sampling strategies, next-state prediction, and partner-action prediction.
The authors report IRB approval and participant compensation for data collection and human studies, which is appropriate for this type of work.
weaknesses: The main empirical claims are not sufficiently convincing. Absolute task completion rates remain low in many settings, and several improvements are modest relative to standard errors. The paper repeatedly claims significant or consistent improvement without enough statistical testing across the main metrics and settings.

The Task 1 evaluation protocol is a weak proxy for adapting to unseen humans. Training two agents on disjoint participant splits and evaluating them against each other measures model-model compatibility, not direct adaptation to new human behavior. This undermines a central claim of the benchmark and method.

The human-study reporting is inconsistent and under-specified: the main text says 32 participants, while Appendix R says 12 volunteers. The study compares only BASS against DP, gives limited detail about randomization/counterbalancing, and reports a single p-value despite multiple questionnaire items.

The behavior augmentation method has questionable validity. Recombining sub-trajectories based on matching one agent's start/end pose does not guarantee physical consistency of the partner trajectory or object/environment state, especially when object movement and collisions are central to the task. The claimed 99% validity is not defined rigorously enough.

The BASS method is more of a combination of known ingredients than a clearly novel algorithmic contribution: data augmentation, learned dynamics/next-state prediction, candidate action sampling, and reward-based selection are familiar ideas. The novelty is mainly in the benchmark, but the method is presented with stronger claims than the evidence supports.

The benchmark's scope is narrower than the framing suggests. It is a 2D game-like simulator based on Pymunk/MAGICAL, yet the paper repeatedly uses language such as physically grounded, realistic physics, and real-world applicability. The gap to actual embodied robots is not adequately discussed.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many appendix details. The project URL is missing in the extracted manuscript, and important details such as data/code availability, exact train/test splits, human-study assignment, filtering of low-quality demonstrations, and full statistical procedures are not sufficiently specified.

The comparison to MAPPO is not very persuasive. The paper acknowledges that the benchmark was designed around dataset-driven methods, then adapts MAPPO with dense rewards and map-specific changes. This makes it hard to interpret the RL baseline as a strong or fair representative of reinforcement learning approaches.

The limitations discussion is too shallow. The paper does not adequately address simulator-to-real transfer, dependence on dense state information, brittleness of learned dynamics under distribution shift, costs of diffusion-policy inference plus action selection, or the possibility that BASS optimizes the chosen NFD metric rather than genuinely improving collaboration.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: there are typos and inconsistencies such as BAAS/BASS, participant count mismatch, missing project-page link, and some overclaiming relative to the reported evidence. These are not merely cosmetic because they affect interpretation of reproducibility and empirical reliability.

strengths: The paper makes a meaningful contribution by introducing Moving Out, a physically grounded human-AI collaboration benchmark with continuous low-level control, object physics, varied map types, and human-human demonstrations. This fills a real gap between symbolic collaboration benchmarks such as Overcooked-AI and more physically constrained embodied collaboration settings.

The experimental evaluation is broad and mostly convincing: the authors evaluate adaptation to unseen human behaviors, generalization to unseen physical attributes, AI-AI cross-group performance, human-AI interaction, survey feedback, failure modes, and several ablations of BASS components.

BASS is a practical and well-motivated method: behavior augmentation addresses limited/diverse human data, while learned next-state prediction and candidate action selection directly target physical feasibility. The oracle-simulator comparison, sampling ablation, partner-action ablation, and alternative dynamics-model comparisons strengthen the soundness of the method claims.

The human data collection is a major asset. The paper reports IRB approval, participant compensation, dataset sizes, diversity metrics, and map/task design details. The benchmark itself is likely to be useful for future work even beyond the proposed method.

Presentation is generally clear, with good figures, intuitive task descriptions, and detailed appendices covering metrics, implementation, compute, MAPPO reward shaping, data collection, and questionnaire design.
weaknesses: The human-study reporting is inconsistent: the main text states 32 participants, while Appendix R states 12 volunteers. This is a material reproducibility and interpretation issue, especially because human-AI performance is one of the central pieces of evidence.

The primary Task 1 reproducible protocol uses AI agents trained on disjoint human splits and then paired with each other as a proxy for unseen human behavior. This is reasonable, but it is still only an indirect proxy for real human adaptation, and the paper sometimes phrases the resulting evidence more strongly than the protocol warrants.

Reproducibility is not fully established from the manuscript alone. The abstract says the project page is available but appears to omit the actual URL, and it is unclear whether the environment, dataset, trained models, and evaluation scripts will be released in a form sufficient to reproduce the benchmark and results.

Some empirical gains, especially in AI-AI settings, are moderate relative to the standard errors, and the paper does not consistently report significance tests for task metrics. The strongest improvements are in human play, but those are also where the participant-count inconsistency matters most.

The method is partly benchmark-specific: action selection uses NFD based on object-goal distances and BFS over known map structure, and the dynamics model is trained in the same simulator domain. The paper includes a small Overcooked result, but the broader generality of BASS remains only lightly supported.

Limitations are discussed mainly as future work and failure cases rather than as a consolidated limitations section. Important constraints such as 2D simulation, joystick-based participants, limited participant diversity, 10% physical randomization, and transfer to real robots should be more explicitly framed.
